## 1. Safety, legal and status disclaimer

This scheme is **decision-support and management documentation**. It **must be reviewed and signed off by a competent person** (a qualified aviation SME / the accountable post-holders) before adoption, and reviewed periodically thereafter. It is **not legal advice** and does not itself grant any legal immunity.

Where this document describes legal or regulatory protection for reporters, that protection derives from — and is limited by — the applicable DGCA Civil Aviation Requirements, India's State Safety Programme (SSP), and the Operator's Just Culture Policy. **No part of this scheme overrides any lawful order of a court, the DGCA, or the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB), nor does it relieve the Operator of any mandatory occurrence-reporting obligation.**

Exact regulatory instrument numbers carrying a **[GAP]** flag in this document must be verified against the current DGCA CAR text before the scheme is adopted.

---

## 2. Purpose and objectives

The Confidential Safety Reporting Scheme (CSRS) is the Operator's **voluntary, confidential** channel for surfacing safety hazards, latent conditions, human-factors issues and near-misses that the **mandatory occurrence-reporting (MOR)** system does not, or would not, otherwise capture — reported by any member of the workforce **without fear of identification or reprisal**.

**Objectives**

1. Capture hazards and precursors *before* they cause an occurrence, especially those a reporter would not raise through their line manager or the mandatory channel.
2. Guarantee, by **engineered workflow** rather than by promise alone, that a reporter cannot be identified from anything the scheme circulates or acts upon.
3. Feed the Operator's Safety Risk Management process (ICAO Annex 19 Pillar 2) with hazards ranked and mitigated through the **hierarchy of controls**.
4. Close the loop — every reporter learns what happened to their report.
5. Reinforce, and depend upon, the Operator's **Just Culture Policy** — reporting is the mechanism; just culture is the fairness framework.

**This scheme is not** a substitute for mandatory occurrence reporting (see §10), not a grievance or industrial-relations channel, and not a route for allegations of misconduct against named individuals (see §4.4).

## 4. Scheme design

### 4.1 Scheme type

**Confidential** (identity known to a single custodian, protected), with an **anonymous** option available to any reporter who prefers to capture no identity at all.

| Type | Identity captured? | Feedback to reporter possible? | Use in this scheme |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Confidential** *(default)* | Yes — known **only** to the Confidential Reporting Custodian, then de-identified before analysis | Yes — direct, via the Custodian | Primary channel |
| **Anonymous** *(available)* | No | No direct feedback; outcome via the de-identified safety bulletin only | Offered to any reporter who selects it |
| Voluntary/open (non-confidential) | Identity open | Yes | Handled through the normal safety-reporting and line-manager route — **not** this scheme |

The handling workflow (§5–§6) is designed for the **confidential** model and must not be blended with the anonymous model: an anonymous report has **no re-identification key** and receives **bulletin-only** feedback.

### 4.2 What to report through the CSRS

Anything the reporter believes affects safety and would not otherwise be raised, including: hazards and unsafe conditions; latent/organisational weaknesses (procedures, rostering pressure, fatigue, workload, pairing, training gaps); human-factors and human-performance issues; near-misses and "get-away-with-it" events; normalisation of deviation; and concerns the reporter is uncomfortable raising by name.

### 4.3 What still goes to the mandatory channel

Reportable accidents, serious incidents and mandatory occurrences must **always** be filed through the MOR system per DGCA requirements, regardless of whether they are also raised here (see §10). The CSRS **does not discharge** a mandatory-reporting obligation.

### 4.4 What must not be routed here

The CSRS is **not** a channel for allegations of misconduct, harassment or grievance against a named individual. Such matters follow the Operator's HR/grievance process. A confidential *safety* report must describe **hazards and system conditions, not persons** — reporters are asked not to name individuals (§Appendix A guidance). This boundary is what keeps the scheme a safety instrument and not a disciplinary one.

### 4.5 Governance and roles (role-based — no individuals named)

| Role | Responsibility in the CSRS |
|---|---|
| **Accountable Manager** | Owns the confidentiality commitment; approves the scheme; guarantees the Custodian's independence and resources; is the only role who may authorise any deviation, and only per §7.4. |
| **Safety Manager** | Scheme owner; chairs the Confidential Report Review Panel; assures the hierarchy-of-controls response; reports scheme performance to the Safety Review Board. **Never holds reporter identities.** |
| **Confidential Reporting Custodian** | The **single point** at which reporter identity is held. Receives reports, acknowledges reporters, performs de-identification, holds the re-identification key, relays feedback. Independent of line management, rostering, HR and disciplinary functions. |
| **Deputy Confidential Reporting Custodian** | Cover for the Custodian under the same controls; the only other role with register access. |
| **Confidential Report Review Panel** | Multidisciplinary panel (flight ops, cabin, engineering, ground ops, human factors) that risk-assesses and actions **de-identified** reports. **Never sees identities; never contacts reporters directly.** |
| **Compliance Monitoring Manager** | Advises whether an underlying occurrence is separately mandatorily reportable and manages the distinct MOR routing (§10). |
| **Data Protection / Information Security Officer** | Assures the technical isolation, access controls, retention and DPDP-Act alignment of the Confidential Register. |
| **Line / Base Managers** | Receive and act on **de-identified** actions and bulletins; play **no part** in intake, de-identification or identity handling. |
| **The reporter** | Any member of the workforce. Always de-identified. |

**Custodian independence is load-bearing.** The Custodian role must sit outside the disciplinary and rostering chain so that holding a reporter's identity can never be leveraged against them. *[ASSUMPTION: the Custodian is positioned within the Safety Department but firewalled from line management; confirm reporting line at adoption.]*

## 5. Report intake

### 5.1 Intake channels (all terminate **only** at the Custodian)

| Channel | Design control |
|---|---|
| **Web portal** | TLS-encrypted; **no mandatory identity field**; the "how to reach me for feedback" field is optional and delivered only to the Custodian mailbox. No IP/device logging tied to the report body. |
| **Paper form** | Locked drop-boxes at each base + a reply-paid envelope to a Custodian-only PO box; opened only by the Custodian/Deputy. |
| **Confidential hotline / voicemail** | A dedicated line whose mailbox is accessible only by the Custodian/Deputy. |
| **Confidential mailbox / app** | A single mailbox/app inbox monitored only by the Custodian/Deputy. |

**Excluded as a confidential channel:** reporting *through a line manager*. That route cannot be confidential and is reserved for open safety reports. This exclusion is deliberate.

### 5.2 The intake form (design)

The form is deliberately minimal — it collects what is needed to understand the hazard, and no more (data minimisation).

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| Confidential Report Reference (CRR) | **Auto-generated on receipt by the Custodian** — not entered by the reporter |
| What happened | Free text — reporter asked to describe the *hazard/condition*, **not to name individuals** |
| Where / operation type | Captured, then **generalised** at de-identification (e.g., "a line station", "cruise") |
| When | Captured, then **generalised to a window** at de-identification (e.g., "Q2 2026"), never an exact date in the circulated copy |
| Why it happened / contributing factors | Free text |
| Suggested improvement | Free text (optional) |
| Reporter category (optional) | Broad only — flight crew / cabin crew / engineering / ground ops / dispatch / other; generalised further if it could identify |
| Do you want feedback? | Yes/No. If yes → an optional contact method **held only by the Custodian** |
| Consent to publish a de-identified lesson in the safety bulletin? | Yes/No |

The blank form template is at **Appendix A**.

## 6. Intake-to-de-identification handling workflow

**De-identification is load-bearing and happens at the earliest possible point — in the Custodian's hands, before any other role sees the content.** The re-identification key never leaves the Custodian and is never placed in this document or in any circulated artifact.

### 6.1 Step-by-step

| # | Step | Owner | Control |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Receipt & registration** | Custodian | Report received via a Custodian-only channel; a unique **CRR** assigned; the original (identifiable) copy stored in the access-controlled **Confidential Register**. |
| 2 | **Acknowledge the reporter** | Custodian | Within **3 working days** *(SLA, §9)*, the Custodian acknowledges receipt (via the reporter's chosen contact), quotes the CRR and restates the protection promise. |
| 3 | **De-identify (disidentify)** | Custodian | The Custodian creates the **de-identified working copy**: remove/tokenise name and contact; generalise role/fleet-seat/route/base; generalise exact date → window; remove flight number, aircraft registration, roster position and any **narrative detail that could triangulate** the reporter (a determined reader test is applied). |
| 4 | **Split the record** | Custodian | Two artifacts result: **(a)** the de-identified working copy (goes forward) and **(b)** the **re-identification key** entry `CRR ↔ identity`, which **stays in the Confidential Register only**. |
| 5 | **Hand to analysis** | Custodian → Safety Manager / Panel | **Only** the de-identified working copy is released. The key is never handed over. |
| 6 | **Risk-assess & determine action** | Review Panel | Score the hazard on the ICAO 5×5 Risk Classification Scheme; determine mitigations **ranked by the hierarchy of controls** (§8); assign a named-**role** owner and a target date. |
| 7 | **Follow-up (if needed)** | Panel → Custodian → reporter | If the Panel needs more detail, it asks the **Custodian** to relay the question. **The Panel never contacts the reporter directly.** |
| 8 | **Mandatory-reporting check** | Compliance Monitoring Manager (via Custodian) | Determine whether the underlying occurrence is separately mandatorily reportable; if so, route via MOR **on a de-identified basis** (§10). The confidential channel never becomes the reporter's identifier to the regulator. |
| 9 | **Feedback** | Custodian relays; Safety Manager authors | Outcome fed back to the reporter via the Custodian; a de-identified lesson published in the safety bulletin **with the reporter's consent** (§9). |
| 10 | **Closure, retention & key disposal** | Custodian | CRR closed; de-identified record retained per §12; **the re-identification key is destroyed once ongoing feedback is no longer required** — identity is not retained longer than its purpose. |
| 11 | **Independent audit** | Data Protection / Info-Sec Officer | Periodic audit of the *process and access logs* (never the identities) to assure the controls are working. |

### 6.2 The Confidential Register (identity store) — access controls

- Encrypted, access-controlled store, **logically and physically separated** from HR, flight-ops, rostering/crew-scheduling and disciplinary systems — **no automated linkage**.
- Access limited to the **Custodian and Deputy** only; every access logged (immutable audit trail reviewed by the Data Protection / Info-Sec Officer).
- No export of identities to any downstream tool; the SMS hazard database receives **only** de-identified working copies.
- A "break-glass" access is possible **only** under §7.4 (the just-culture exception), is fully logged, and requires the Accountable Manager's authorisation.
- Aligned to the DPDP Act, 2023: minimise, limit to purpose, and delete when the purpose ends.

### 6.3 Anonymous variant

If the reporter selected **anonymous**, Steps 1–2 capture **no identity**, Step 4 produces **no key**, Steps 7 and 9 provide **no direct feedback** (bulletin only), and Step 10 has **no key to destroy**. The workflow must not silently treat an anonymous report as confidential.

---

## 7. Confidentiality and protection commitment

### 7.1 The promise (mechanical, not aspirational)

> **"You can report without being identified."** Your identity is known only to the Confidential Reporting Custodian. Before anyone else sees your report, it is de-identified. No line manager, HR function, or member of the Review Panel receives your identity. Your report will **not** be used to start or support disciplinary or enforcement action against you, within the limits of the Just Culture Policy (§7.3).

This promise is backed by the workflow steps in §6 and the controls below — **not by trust alone**.

### 7.2 Protection controls — ranked by the hierarchy of controls

Applied to the hazard of *reporter re-identification*:

1. **Elimination** — the **anonymous option**: where the reporter chooses it, no identity is captured, so there is nothing to protect.
2. **Substitution** — **de-identify at the earliest point** (§6, Step 3): downstream handlers work only with de-identified data.
3. **Engineering** — technical isolation: Custodian-only channels; encrypted, access-controlled Register; the re-identification key held **separately** and never circulated; **no linkage** to rostering/HR; role-based access; immutable audit logging.
4. **Administrative** — the confidentiality policy; the Custodian appointment and independence; confidentiality undertakings for the Custodian/Deputy/Panel; training; the **disciplinary firewall** (§7.3); the retention-and-disposal schedule (§12).
5. **PPE (individual last line)** — reporter guidance: *do not name individuals; do not include detail that identifies you* (Appendix A).

> **Lower-order control flag.** A purely administrative promise ("management undertakes not to look") is **not** an adequate control on its own — justify why higher-order isolation is not reasonably practicable, or engineer it in. This scheme engineers it in (level 3), and does **not** rely on administrative assurance alone.

### 7.3 The disciplinary firewall and the just-culture boundary

- A confidential report is **inadmissible** as the trigger for, or evidence in, disciplinary or enforcement action against the reporter.
- **Boundary (protection does not extend to):** deliberate/willful violation, gross negligence, reckless conduct, criminal act, sabotage, or being under the influence of alcohol/psychoactive substances. These are adjudicated through the **Just Culture Policy decision tree**, not by the Custodian.
- Even where the boundary may be engaged, **the Custodian does not unilaterally disclose identity.** Any lifting of protection follows §7.4.

### 7.4 The exception process (high threshold, documented, not a backdoor)

Reporter identity may be accessed **only** where: (a) required by a lawful order of a court, the DGCA, or the AAIB; **or** (b) the Just Culture Policy process determines the just-culture boundary (§7.3) is engaged. In either case: the **Accountable Manager** authorises; the access is **logged**; the reporter is informed **where lawful to do so**; and the decision is recorded. The existence of this narrow, high-threshold exception is disclosed to reporters up front (§Appendix C) — **the scheme does not promise a protection the law does not grant.**

### 7.5 What the scheme cannot promise

The scheme cannot and does not promise immunity from investigation or prosecution, cannot override a lawful disclosure order, and does not remove the Operator's mandatory-reporting duties. Stating otherwise would be a false assurance.

## 8. Acting on reports — hierarchy of controls

When a confidential report surfaces a hazard, the Review Panel must determine the response by the **hierarchy of controls**, most effective first — **elimination → substitution → engineering → administrative → PPE** — with each control tied to the specific hazard and its level.

- A response that defaults to *"issue a notice / remind crews / add a briefing"* (administrative-only) or *"wear/use X"* (PPE-only) must carry the flag: **"Lower-order control — justify why a higher-order control (elimination / substitution / engineering) is not reasonably practicable, or escalate."**
- Every action is assigned a **named-role owner** and a **target/review date**, and tracked to closure — the same discipline as any SMS corrective action.

*Worked illustration (illustrative — not a real report):* a confidential report that turnaround time pressure is driving rushed pre-flight walk-arounds. **Administrative-only** ("remind crews to take their time") is flagged as insufficient; higher-order options — **eliminate/substitute** the pressure by re-timing the ground programme, **engineer** a protected minimum turnaround buffer into scheduling — are considered first, with the administrative reminder as a supplement, not the treatment.

---

## 9. Feedback loop to reporters

A report with no feedback erodes trust and the scheme dies. Feedback is therefore mandatory and measured.

| Stage | SLA | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| **Acknowledge receipt** (CRR issued) | **3 working days** *[ASSUMPTION — confirm at adoption]* | Custodian |
| **Interim update** (if not yet closed) | **30 days**, then monthly | Custodian (content from Safety Manager) |
| **Outcome / closure feedback** | On closure of the CRR | Custodian relays; Safety Manager authors |

**Two feedback routes (per intake choice):**

1. **Direct to the reporter, via the Custodian** — for confidential reporters who requested feedback. The Custodian is the relay; the Safety Manager never learns who received it.
2. **De-identified safety bulletin** ("Feedback" publication, CHIRP/ASRS-style) — periodic, published to all staff, carrying the lesson and the action taken. Published **only** with the reporter's consent for that report.

**Safety-bulletin de-identification rules.** The bulletin carries no names, no exact dates, no route/registration/roster detail. It **aggregates** — no category with **fewer than 5** individuals/reports is published as a distinct cell, and secondary suppression is applied so a suppressed small cell cannot be back-calculated from totals. A sample bulletin entry is at **Appendix B**.

---

## 10. Interface with mandatory occurrence reporting (MOR)

The confidential scheme and the mandatory channel are **distinct and must never blur.** The CSRS captures voluntary hazard/precursor information; the MOR system captures occurrences the Operator is **legally required** to report to the DGCA/AAIB.

| Dimension | Confidential Safety Reporting Scheme (CSRS) | Mandatory Occurrence Reporting (MOR) |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Voluntary hazards, precursors, human-factors, near-misses | Legally reportable accidents/serious incidents/occurrences |
| Trigger | A reporter chooses to report | An occurrence meets a mandatory threshold |
| Identity | Confidential (Custodian-only), or anonymous | Attributable operational report; not confidential in the same sense |
| Legal basis | DGCA voluntary-reporting/SMS provisions + SSP just culture *[GAP: confirm CAR]* | DGCA mandatory-reporting CAR + Aircraft (Investigation of Accidents and Incidents) Rules, 2017 *[GAP: confirm citations]* |
| Timeframe | Feedback SLA (§9); no statutory filing clock | Statutory reporting deadlines to DGCA/AAIB *[GAP: confirm]* |
| Owner | Confidential Reporting Custodian / Safety Manager | Compliance Monitoring Manager / accountable post-holder |
| Protection | Reporter protected per §7 | Occurrence reported on the merits |

**Where a confidential report reveals a mandatorily reportable occurrence:**

1. The mandatory-reporting obligation is triggered by **the occurrence itself**, not by the confidential report. Where the occurrence is already known operationally, the MOR is filed through the normal mandatory channel independently of the CSRS.
2. Where a mandatorily reportable condition is surfaced **only** through the confidential channel, the Operator still meets its duty — the Compliance Monitoring Manager files the mandatory report **using the de-identified working copy**, so the confidential channel does not become the mechanism that identifies the reporter to the regulator.
3. The Operator does **not** use the CSRS as a way to avoid or delay a mandatory report. *[ASSUMPTION/GAP: confirm with the DGCA whether a de-identified mandatory filing is acceptable in the specific case; if the regulator requires attributable detail, the just-culture exception (§7.4) governs — the Custodian does not disclose unilaterally.]*

## 11. Interface with the Just Culture Policy

The CSRS is the **reporting mechanism**; the **Just Culture Policy** is the fairness framework that decides how the Operator *responds* to what is reported. They are designed together and are mutually dependent.

- **Dependency.** People report confidentially only if they trust the just-culture response. A weak just-culture policy will empty this scheme regardless of how good the confidentiality engineering is.
- **Disciplinary firewall.** Confidential reports are inadmissible against the reporter (§7.3), consistent with the just-culture commitment.
- **The boundary and the decision tree.** The exclusions in §7.3 are adjudicated through the Just Culture Policy's **substitution test / decision tree** (see the Operator's `aviation-just-culture-policy`), not by the Custodian and not by line management acting alone.
- **Escalation, not identification.** Where a report's *content* (never its source) indicates a systemic issue requiring management action, the de-identified working copy escalates through the SMS — the reporter's identity does not travel with it.
- **Governance.** Scheme performance and any §7.4 exception events are reported to the **Safety Review Board**, maintaining the link between Pillar 4 (this scheme) and Pillar 1 (safety policy and accountabilities).

## 12. Records, retention and data protection

| Record | Retention | Control |
|---|---|---|
| De-identified working copies / SMS hazard records | *[ASSUMPTION: 5 years, then fully anonymise/archive — GAP: confirm against DGCA record-keeping requirements]* | Held in the SMS hazard database; no identities present |
| Re-identification key (`CRR ↔ identity`) | **Minimised** — destroyed once ongoing feedback is no longer required *[ASSUMPTION: default destroy at CRR closure — GAP: confirm]* | Confidential Register only; Custodian/Deputy access; logged |
| Confidential Register access log | *[GAP: confirm retention]* | Immutable; audited by Data Protection / Info-Sec Officer |
| Safety bulletins | Indefinite (already de-identified/aggregated) | Public to staff |

Handling of the identity register aligns to the **DPDP Act, 2023**: collect the minimum, use only for the reporting purpose, store no longer than needed, and delete on purpose completion. **Cells of fewer than 5** are never published (§9).

## 13. Performance monitoring and assurance (Pillar 3)

Scheme health is measured and reported to the Safety Review Board. A **falling report rate** is treated as a warning about trust, not as good news.

| SPI | Indicator | Direction | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| SPI-CR-01 | Report rate (reports per month / per 1,000 flying hours) | Watch — a fall may signal lost trust | Safety Manager |
| SPI-CR-02 | Reports acknowledged within SLA (%) | Higher is better; target 100% | Custodian |
| SPI-CR-03 | Reports closed with feedback to reporter (%) | Higher is better | Safety Manager |
| SPI-CR-04 | Median time to close | Lower is better | Safety Manager |
| SPI-CR-05 | Reporter-confidence index (periodic anonymous pulse survey) | Higher is better | Safety Manager |
| SPI-CR-06 | Confidentiality breaches | **Zero.** Any breach is a de-identification incident — investigated as a serious event | Data Protection / Info-Sec Officer |

*[ASSUMPTION: alert/target levels to be set against the Operator's baseline once data exists — none captured at intake.]*

## Appendix A — Confidential Safety Report form (template)

> **Your identity is protected.** This form reaches only the Confidential Reporting Custodian. Please describe the *hazard or situation* — **do not name individuals**, and leave out any detail that would identify you if you would rather stay unidentifiable.

- **Confidential Report Reference (CRR):** *(assigned by the Custodian — leave blank)*
- **What happened?** *(the hazard / unsafe condition / near-miss)*
- **Where / what kind of operation?** *(e.g., a line station, cruise, turnaround — no need to be exact)*
- **When?** *(approximate is fine — e.g., "last month")*
- **Why do you think it happened?** *(contributing factors)*
- **What would make it safer?** *(your suggestion — optional)*
- **Your area (optional, broad):** ☐ Flight crew ☐ Cabin crew ☐ Engineering ☐ Ground ops ☐ Dispatch ☐ Other
- **Do you want feedback?** ☐ Yes → *how may the Custodian reach you? (held only by the Custodian)* ______  ☐ No
- **May we publish a de-identified lesson from this report in the safety bulletin?** ☐ Yes ☐ No
- **Report type:** ☐ Confidential (identity held only by the Custodian) ☐ Anonymous (no identity captured; bulletin feedback only)

## Appendix B — Sample de-identified safety-bulletin entry (illustrative)

> **CSRS Feedback — Issue [n], [Month] 2026**
> **What was reported:** Concerns that compressed turnaround times at line stations were pressuring crews during pre-departure checks.
> **What we did:** The Review Panel assessed the hazard and, rather than a reminder alone (flagged as a lower-order control), the ground-programme timings are being reviewed and a protected minimum turnaround buffer is being trialled (higher-order: engineer out the time pressure). Owner: Ground Operations lead role. Target review: [Month] 2026.
> **Thank you** to the reporter. Keep reporting — confidentially.

*(No names, no dates beyond the month, no route/registration; aggregated so no cell < 5.)*

## Appendix C — Reporter protection statement (plain-language, for crew rooms/portal)

> **Report it. Confidentially.**
> Your name is seen by **one person only** — the Confidential Reporting Custodian — and is removed before anyone else reads your report. **No line manager, HR or review-panel member gets your identity.** Your report **won't be used against you** — that's our just-culture promise. The only exceptions, set by law and our Just Culture Policy, are a lawful order from a court/DGCA/AAIB, or conduct that crosses the just-culture line (deliberate harm, gross negligence, criminal acts, or being under the influence) — and even then your identity isn't disclosed by the Custodian alone. **We can't promise legal immunity, and mandatory occurrences still have to be reported — but we can, and do, protect your identity.** You'll always hear back.
